title: Hotel Reservation System
problem: Design a hotel reservation system (Booking.com / Expedia / direct hotel chain) that takes rooms from search, through hold, payment, and confirmed booking, without overselling.
summary: A consistency-critical booking pipeline: search is read-heavy and can be served from a denormalized availability cache; booking is write-critical and must never oversell. The design uses Redis for short-lived room holds (SETNX with TTL) plus idempotency keys, a strongly-consistent SQL database (MySQL / Postgres / Aurora) for the authoritative reservation + inventory tables, and an external payment provider (Stripe-style) with network-grade idempotency. The dominant design choice is 'hold then confirm' over optimistic 'book directly' — holds keep inventory reserved for 10 min during checkout so the user can enter payment details without the room disappearing or double-selling. The main tradeoff is locked but unpaid inventory during the hold window; bookable-room utilization is slightly reduced in exchange for a clean UX and a hard no-oversell guarantee.

functional: Search hotels and room types by destination, dates, and guest count
Place a short-lived hold on a specific room while the user enters payment
Confirm a booking atomically with a successful payment authorization
Support idempotent POST /bookings via client-supplied Idempotency-Key
Cancel and refund bookings subject to the hotel cancellation policy
Email and push confirmation to the guest and notification to the hotel
nonFunctional: No oversell under any concurrency pattern; correctness is a hard constraint
Search p95 under 500 ms, hold p95 under 200 ms, booking p95 under 2 s (payment-bound)
Availability 99.95% for search, 99.99% for the booking pipeline
Hold TTL 10 minutes with a one-click extend option
Reservation DB survives a full AZ failure without losing committed bookings

assumptions: 1M hotels globally, avg 200 rooms each → 200M room-nights inventory
Avg checkout session 4 min; hold TTL = 10 min (buffer for payment)
No-oversell is a hard constraint — correctness > availability
Payment SLA: external provider p95 ≈ 600ms, p99 ≈ 1.5s
estimates: Booking QPS: 1M / 86400 ≈ 12 sustained, ~50 peak — tiny absolute numbers, the challenge is correctness not scale
Active holds at any moment: 50 QPS * 10 min = 30K concurrent holds max
Reservation DB row count: 900K/day * 365 * 5yr ≈ 1.6B rows (partitioned by check_in month)
Redis footprint: 30K holds * ~1 KB ≈ 30 MB — trivial

architecture.mermaid: graph LR client[Client] --> lb[Load Balancer] lb --> api[Reservation API] api --> search[Search Service] api --> inventory[Inventory Service] api --> redis[(Redis Holds + Idempotency)] inventory --> db[(Reservation DB)] api --> payment[Payment Provider] api --> notify[Notification Service]

client.name: Client (Web / Mobile)
client.summary: Browser or mobile app that drives search → room detail → checkout → confirmation.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- GET /search?dest=...&checkin=...&checkout=...&guests=N
- POST /holds (lock a room during checkout)
- POST /bookings (with Idempotency-Key header)
- GET /bookings/:id (confirmation page; also used for retry-safe polling)

sections.heading: Idempotency-Key on client
sections.body: Before POST /bookings the client generates a UUID and sends it in the `Idempotency-Key` header. The same UUID is used on every retry of the same logical booking. Stripe, PayPal, and Booking's own API all follow this pattern.

sections.heading: Latency expectations
sections.body:
- Search: < 500 ms p95
- Hold: < 200 ms p95
- Book (including payment): < 2 s p95 (dominated by external payment)

bottlenecks.title: Hold countdown desync causes failed bookings at submit time
bottlenecks.trigger: User takes longer than the 10-minute hold TTL to enter payment (slow typing, 3DS challenge, tab backgrounded). At 50 peak booking QPS with 30K concurrent holds, even a small % of slow checkouts produces thousands of expired-hold submissions per day.
bottlenecks.symptom: User submits POST /bookings and gets 409 hold_expired after already typing card details; perceived as 'the site stole my room'. Support tickets spike and conversion drops on mobile where SCA adds 30–90s.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Client-side countdown timer synced to server `expires_at`; at T-2min show a warning and offer one-click hold extension (POST /holds/:token/extend) that re-SETNX with a fresh 600s TTL if keys are still owned. Auto-save checkout form to localStorage keyed by hold_token so a re-hold + resubmit is one click.
bottlenecks.detection: Track client metric `booking_submit_after_hold_expiry_ratio` and server 409 rate on POST /bookings by reason=hold_expired; alert when >1% over 5min window.

bottlenecks.title: Idempotency-Key reuse/regeneration bugs causing double-charges or stuck retries
bottlenecks.trigger: Client regenerates UUID on React re-render or retry (double-charge risk), or conversely reuses a key across logically different attempts after a decline (stuck 402 replay from idem cache TTL=24h). Manifests on flaky mobile networks where retries are common.
bottlenecks.symptom: Either duplicate bookings/charges for the same guest (key regenerated on retry) or user sees 'card declined' repeatedly even after entering a new card (stale idem key replays cached 402 response for 24h).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Generate Idempotency-Key once per logical booking attempt and persist in sessionStorage keyed by hold_token; tie key lifecycle to the hold, not the HTTP request. On any user-facing error that requires input change (declined card, edited guest info), explicitly rotate the key. Add an invariant test in the client: same hold_token + same payload ⇒ same key; any payload change ⇒ new key.
bottlenecks.detection: Server-side metric: count of distinct Idempotency-Keys per (user_id, hold_token) — should be exactly 1 for success paths. Alert on >1.05 avg. Also log Idempotency-Key cache hits returning 402 and correlate with user retry count.

bottlenecks.title: Search response payload and CDN miss latency on mobile
bottlenecks.trigger: Search returns up to 20 hotel cards with images, amenities, and room-type arrays. At 350 sustained / 1.2K peak search QPS, CDN miss on long-tail destination+date combos (60s TTL) bypasses the cache and hits the 500ms p95 search budget on slow mobile networks.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users on 3G/4G see 2–4s blank results screen; bounce rate on search page climbs; search-to-hold funnel drops especially in emerging markets.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Client sends `Accept-Encoding: br`, requests thumbnail image URLs (not full-res), and paginates to 10 cards initially with infinite scroll. Use stale-while-revalidate with service worker so repeat searches render in <100ms from cache while refreshing in background. Prefetch room-detail on card hover/viewport-enter to hide hold latency.
bottlenecks.detection: RUM metric for `search_ttfb_p95` and `search_lcp_p95` segmented by connection type (effectiveType from NetworkInformation API); alert when mobile p95 >1.5s for 10min.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the client matters in a hotel booking system In a hotel reservation system, the client isn't just a dumb renderer — it's actually an active participant in the no-oversell guarantee. The client has to generate and persist the `Idempotency-Key` across retries, run the 10-minute hold countdown timer, and know when to ask for a hold extension. If the client gets any of this wrong, the server's careful Redis-plus-SQL machinery can still produce double-charges or "stole my room" experiences. Booking.com-scale systems push this logic to the client because the alternative — the server guessing whether a retry is "the same attempt" — is impossible without a client-supplied key. ## What happens without a smart client Imagine a naive client that regenerates a fresh UUID on every React re-render. The user taps "Book" on a flaky 4G connection, the request times out, the app retries — but now with a *different* idempotency key. The payment provider sees two distinct charges and bills the card twice. The operator sees a spike in duplicate-booking support tickets; the SQL inventory table shows two rows for the same guest; the payment service takes the reputational hit even though it did exactly what it was told. ## The number Capacity says **1M booking attempts/day** against a payment provider with **p99 ≈ 1.5s** and **~0.5% transient error rate**. That's 1,000,000 × 0.005 = **5,000 retries per day** where client idempotency behavior is load-bearing. Get it wrong 1% of the time and you're double-charging 50 guests daily. ## Trade-off Pushing idempotency and hold-timer logic into the client means more frontend complexity and tighter client-server contract discipline — but it's the only place a "logical booking attempt" can actually be defined.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 HTTPS load balancer in front of the reservation API tier.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Least-connections with health checks every 5s. Sticky sessions are NOT used — the API is stateless and all checkout state lives in Redis keyed by the client's `hold_token`.

sections.heading: TLS + WAF
sections.body: Terminates TLS and runs a WAF for basic SQLi / XSS filtering before traffic reaches the API.

sections.heading: Rate limiting
sections.body: Per-IP rate limit: 60 searches/min, 10 booking attempts/min — blocks obvious scrapers and scripted oversell attempts.

bottlenecks.title: TLS handshake CPU saturation during search traffic spikes
bottlenecks.trigger: At 1.2K peak search QPS plus mobile clients with short-lived connections (no keep-alive reuse across app backgrounding), full TLS handshakes dominate LB CPU. A flash sale or marketing push can 3–5x search QPS in seconds, pushing ECDHE handshake cost (~1–2ms CPU each) past available cores.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU pegs at 100%, TLS handshake latency climbs from ~20ms to 200ms+, users see blank search pages and spinners; healthy upstream API replicas sit idle because requests never arrive.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS session resumption (session tickets + session ID cache, 24h lifetime), enforce HTTP/2 with long-lived connections from clients, pre-provision for 3x peak (not 1x), and offload to hardware-accelerated TLS (AWS NLB+ALB or Envoy with BoringSSL AES-NI). Set `ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:50m` equivalent.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB CPU > 70% for 2min, TLS handshake p95 > 50ms, and new-connection-rate/reused-connection-rate ratio > 0.3 (indicating poor session resumption).

bottlenecks.title: Per-IP rate limit false positives behind corporate NAT / mobile CGNAT
bottlenecks.trigger: Rate limit is 60 searches/min and 10 bookings/min per IP. Mobile carriers (CGNAT) and corporate offices share a single egress IP across thousands of users. A travel agency or a crowded airport wifi easily exceeds 60 searches/min collectively, and during peak season this is the norm, not the exception.
bottlenecks.symptom: Legitimate users on mobile networks get HTTP 429 on search or — worse — on the booking submission itself, right after entering card details. Support sees clustered complaints from specific ISPs or enterprise customers; conversion drops in specific geos.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Key rate limits by (IP + user_id) or (IP + session_cookie) for authenticated flows; keep pure-IP limits only for unauthenticated search and raise to 300/min with burst. Whitelist known CGNAT ranges from major carriers. For bookings, rate-limit by user_id + payment_token_fingerprint, not IP.
bottlenecks.detection: Track 429 rate segmented by `X-Forwarded-For` /24 and by ASN; alert when a single ASN accounts for >5% of 429s over 10min, indicating shared-NAT false positives.

bottlenecks.title: Health check flapping drains booking-in-flight connections
bottlenecks.trigger: 5s health checks with default 2-of-3 failure threshold mean a GC pause, a slow SQL query, or brief Redis hiccup on an API replica can mark it unhealthy within 10–15s. At 50 peak booking QPS with booking requests taking up to 2s (payment hop), a drained replica kills ~100 in-flight requests, some mid-payment-call.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users get 502/504 mid-booking; payment may have succeeded at the provider but the API never returned to commit the DB row. On-call sees orphaned charges in reconciliation reports and `booking_submit_failed` spikes correlated with LB deregistration events.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use connection draining with 30s grace period (longer than payment p99 of 1.5s plus margin); health check path `/health/shallow` that only verifies process liveness, not downstream deps; require 3-of-5 failures over 15s before deregistering. Return 503 from API during graceful shutdown so LB stops sending new work before killing in-flight.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB target deregistration rate > 1/min sustained, and correlate `payment_succeeded_without_booking_row` reconciliation metric with deregistration timestamps.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a load balancer sits in front of the hotel reservation API The Reservation API is **stateless** by design — every piece of booking state (holds, idempotency keys, inventory, bookings) lives in Redis or SQL, not in API memory. That's a deliberate choice for this problem because bookings must never be lost to a single server crash mid-checkout. But stateless only pays off if you can run many API replicas and spread traffic across them, and something has to do that spreading. That "something" is the load balancer. It also terminates TLS (so API replicas don't burn CPU on handshakes), runs a WAF, and rate-limits obvious scrapers — the kind of traffic that, for a hotel site, is constant because competitors scrape prices all day. ## What happens without it Point DNS at a single API box and you get two failure modes. First, that box becomes a single point of failure — when it restarts for a deploy, every in-flight checkout gets a connection reset, and users who just entered card details see a blank error page. Second, a burst of scraper traffic or a flash sale pegs its CPU, search latency balloons past the 500ms p95 budget, and legitimate bookings time out while holding Redis locks that then expire — creating the "stole my room" experience the whole hold-then-confirm design was meant to prevent. ## The number Search runs at **~350 QPS sustained, ~1.2K peak**. A single API replica comfortably handles maybe 300 QPS of search work, so you need at least 4 replicas at peak plus headroom for deploys — 1200 / 300 = 4, round up to 6. Without an LB, there's no way to fan traffic across those 6 boxes with health-checked failover. ## The trade-off You accept one more hop (~1–2ms) and one more piece of infrastructure to operate, in exchange for horizontal scalability and zero-downtime deploys of the API tier.

api.name: Reservation API
api.summary: Stateless orchestrator that composes search, inventory, payment, and notifications into the booking workflow.

sections.heading: Endpoints
Hold-then-confirm flow
sections.body:
1. Create hold: Redis SETNX `hold:{hotel}:{room_type}:{date}` with TTL 10m and a server-issued hold_token
2. Client completes checkout details; finalizes booking
3. On POST /bookings: validate hold_token, check idempotency-key cache, start DB txn, call payment, commit txn, release hold, send email

sections.heading: Orchestration safety
sections.body:
- If payment succeeds but the DB commit fails → retry the DB commit with the payment charge_id (the booking's natural dedupe key is charge_id).
- If DB commits but the confirmation email fails → email is sent from an outbox row, retried by a worker. Never block the user on email.

sections.heading: Stateless scaling
sections.body: All state external (Redis, SQL, payment). 50 peak booking QPS is trivial; horizontal scale purely for search traffic.

gained: Per-channel API shaping — mobile BFF can bundle search + hotel detail in one call
lost: Two services to evolve; risk of logic drift

bottlenecks.title: Payment hop holds API worker threads, exhausting booking concurrency
bottlenecks.trigger: POST /bookings blocks on the external payment provider for p95 600ms, p99 1.5s, occasionally 3s+ for 3DS/SCA. At 50 peak booking QPS × 1.5s = 75 in-flight workers just for payment; a provider slowdown to 3s pushes this to 150+, approaching the provider's 200 concurrent in-flight pool limit and saturating API worker threads.
bottlenecks.symptom: API replicas show near-100% worker utilization during payment provider latency spikes; new /bookings requests queue at the LB and eventually time out at 504; search traffic on the same replicas (sharing the worker pool) also slows despite being unrelated work.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Isolate /bookings onto a dedicated worker pool or dedicated API replicas so slow payment calls can't starve /search and /holds. Use async I/O (e.g., Netty/async Python) so a 1.5s payment wait doesn't pin a thread. Set an aggressive payment client timeout (3s) with `GET /charges/{idempotency_key}` reconciliation on timeout rather than blind retry. Bulkhead: cap concurrent payment calls per API replica at ~40 so one replica can't consume the whole provider quota.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when `payment_call_duration_p99` > 2s for 2min, `api_worker_pool_utilization` > 80%, or `payment_inflight_concurrent` > 150 globally. Track `/bookings` 504 rate and correlate with payment provider latency.

bottlenecks.title: Orphaned charges when payment succeeds but DB commit fails
bottlenecks.trigger: Between the payment provider returning `charge succeeded` and the SQL BEGIN/COMMIT finishing, the API replica can crash, lose DB connectivity, or hit a deadlock on `room_inventory` UPDATE. At 900K successful bookings/day with a 0.05% API failure rate, that's ~450 orphaned charges/day where the guest's card was charged but no booking row exists.
bottlenecks.symptom: Guest's card is charged but no confirmation email arrives and `GET /bookings/:id` returns 404; support tickets for 'I was charged but have no reservation'; reconciliation job flags charge_ids in the payment provider with no matching `bookings.charge_id`.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Persist an intent row (`bookings` status='pending' with idempotency_key UNIQUE) in SQL BEFORE calling payment; the commit after payment only flips status to 'confirmed' and writes charge_id. On recovery, a sweeper reconciles pending rows by calling `GET /charges/{idempotency_key}` on the provider: if charged, flip to confirmed and emit outbox; if not, mark failed and release hold. Use the idempotency_key as the shared dedupe handle across API + payment + DB.
bottlenecks.detection: Reconciliation job compares payment provider charges (last 1h) against `bookings.charge_id`; alert on any `charge_without_booking` count > 0. Metric `bookings_pending_older_than_5min` should be near zero.

bottlenecks.title: Idempotency-key race: concurrent retries bypass the in-flight guard
bottlenecks.trigger: Client on flaky mobile network fires a retry before the first request finishes. The `in_flight` marker is SET NX EX=30, but payment can take up to 1.5s and the DB txn another 25ms — within that window a retry that arrives on a DIFFERENT API replica sees `in_flight` and returns 409, even though the original is still legitimately processing. At 1M booking attempts/day with ~0.5% retry rate, that's 5000 retries/day, a meaningful fraction racing the 1.5s payment window.
bottlenecks.symptom: User sees a confusing 409 'duplicate in flight' on their own retry, then the original succeeds seconds later — or worse, the 30s TTL expires mid-payment and a second retry slips past the guard, triggering a duplicate charge if the payment provider's own idempotency misbehaves.
bottlenecks.mitigation: On `in_flight` hit, don't 409 — long-poll: wait up to 2s for the key to transition to a terminal state, then return that cached result. Extend the in_flight TTL to max(payment_timeout + db_timeout + buffer) = 5s, and refresh it periodically during long payment calls (heartbeat). Always pass the client's Idempotency-Key through to the payment provider unchanged so dual-layer dedupe protects against the TTL-expiry edge case.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `idem_inflight_conflict_count` per minute and `idem_key_ttl_expired_while_processing`; alert if either > 10/min. Log and count any case where the same Idempotency-Key produced two distinct charge_ids at the provider.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Reservation API sits at the center In the hotel reservation system, a single booking isn't one action — it's a *choreography*: check the hold in Redis, call the external payment provider, decrement inventory in SQL, write the booking row, enqueue a confirmation email, and cache the idempotency result. Someone has to run that sequence in the right order, with the right rollback if any step fails. That someone is the Reservation API. It's the only place where "this Idempotency-Key has already been processed, return the cached response" and "payment succeeded but DB commit failed, reconcile with the charge_id" can actually be decided. The client can't do it (it's untrusted and might retry), and neither Redis nor SQL nor Stripe knows about the others. ## What happens without it If the client talked directly to Redis, SQL, and the payment provider, a mid-flight crash would leave the system in a torn state — card charged, no booking row, hold still held. The user sees "something went wrong," their card is debited, support gets a ticket, and the inventory row stays locked until the Redis TTL expires 10 minutes later. Worse, there's nowhere to enforce idempotency, so a mobile retry double-charges. ## The number Capacity says **1M booking attempts/day ≈ 12 QPS sustained, ~50 QPS peak** — trivial throughput. The API exists for *correctness*, not scale: at 0.5% retry rate that's 5,000 retries/day where the API's idempotency-key cache is the only thing preventing duplicate charges. ## Trade-off One extra network hop and an orchestration layer to maintain, in exchange for a single place to enforce the no-oversell and no-double-charge invariants.

search.name: Search Service
search.summary: Elasticsearch-backed availability search indexed nightly from the authoritative inventory.

sections.heading: Index shape
sections.body: Document per (hotel_id, room_type, date_range_block). Fields: location (geo_point), price, amenities, availability_flag, last_indexed_at. Updated by a CDC pipeline on every inventory change.

sections.heading: Why ES (not SQL)
sections.body: Search is geo + faceted + full-text ('hotels within 2km of Eiffel Tower, sea view, free wifi, under €300'). SQL can do it but ES is 10–100x faster on faceted counts and geo radius queries.

sections.heading: Authoritative vs cached
sections.body: ES is best-effort. The API always re-checks availability against the inventory service before creating a hold — search results can be stale by seconds.

sections.heading: Caching
sections.body: CDN-cached responses for popular destination+date combos with 60s TTL — absorbs most of the search QPS at sub-100ms latency.

gained: One fewer system to run; always consistent with inventory
lost: Faceted search + geo + text at scale is painful

bottlenecks.title: CDN cache miss storm on long-tail destination+date combos
bottlenecks.trigger: At 1.2K peak search QPS with 60s CDN TTL, popular combos (Paris/NYC on weekend dates) are well-cached, but long-tail combos — obscure cities, odd date ranges, uncommon filter permutations — have miss rates >80%. If hit rate drops from the expected 90% to 60% during an unusual event (holiday booking surge, travel advisory lifted), origin QPS jumps from ~120 to ~480, a 4x spike against ES.
bottlenecks.symptom: ES p95 climbs from 80ms to 400ms+, search endpoint blows past its 500ms SLO, users on mobile see 2–4s blank result screens. ES node CPU pegs at 90%+ and query queue depth grows; faceted aggregations (amenity counts) are the slowest and start timing out.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a warm L2 cache (Redis) between API and ES with 5-min TTL keyed on normalized query (bbox rounded to ~1km grid, date bucketed). Implement request coalescing (singleflight) so N concurrent identical misses become 1 ES query. Pre-warm top 10K destination+weekend combos via a cron. Cap facet cardinality and disable expensive aggs on deep-paginated requests.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `cdn_hit_ratio < 80%` over 5min, `es_query_p95 > 150ms`, and `es_cpu > 70%`. Track `origin_qps / total_search_qps` — any sustained rise above 15% signals a cache-miss pattern shift.

bottlenecks.title: CDC indexing lag causes stale availability and 'ghost rooms' in results
bottlenecks.trigger: CDC pipeline from SQL inventory to ES runs continuously but can lag during write bursts (e.g., a flash sale burning through inventory, or a reindex backfill). Design notes `last_cdc_lag_s: 45` as typical, but at peak booking (50 QPS × many rooms) or during ES rolling restart, lag can hit several minutes. Rooms shown as `availability_flag=true` have already been booked out.
bottlenecks.symptom: User sees a room in search, clicks through, and POST /holds returns 409 'sold out' — or worse, hold succeeds (Redis has no global view) but the inventory decrement fails at commit, triggering a refund. Support tickets spike for 'the room disappeared between search and checkout'; search-to-hold conversion drops on sold-out-heavy hotels.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Treat ES as advisory only (already called out in design). At search-time, re-verify availability for the top-N results via a fast SQL/inventory lookup before returning them to the client for popular sold-out-prone hotels (where booked_rooms/total_rooms > 0.85). Emit a `stale_if_error` fallback and show 'few rooms left' hints that encourage fast booking. Add a CDC lag SLO: alert when lag > 30s.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `cdc_lag_seconds` (time from SQL commit to ES visibility), alert at >30s for 2min. Monitor `search_to_hold_409_ratio` — sustained rise signals stale index. Compare sampled ES `availability_flag` vs SQL ground truth in a 1% canary job, alert on divergence >1%.

bottlenecks.title: Expensive geo + facet queries drive ES heap pressure and GC pauses
bottlenecks.trigger: Queries combine geo_bounding_box, multiple range filters, and faceted aggregations (amenities, price buckets, star ratings). With 12.4M hotel docs and 20 results × ~10 facet fields per query at 1.2K peak QPS, ES must compute aggregations across potentially 100K+ matching docs per shard. Heap fills with fielddata/doc-values caches; young-gen GC frequency climbs, eventually triggering old-gen pauses.
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic 200–800ms latency spikes uncorrelated with QPS (GC pauses). `took_ms` p99 jumps from 80ms to 1s+. Node logs show `[gc][young][...]` taking >500ms. Occasionally a node drops from the cluster under pressure, causing shard reallocation that further degrades latency for minutes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap facet aggregation to top-N buckets (e.g., `size: 10` on terms aggs), use `execution_hint: map` for low-cardinality fields. Force-merge index to optimal segment count nightly. Use `doc_values: true` (default) and disable `fielddata` on text fields. Scale out to more smaller shards rather than fewer large ones (target <30GB/shard). Set `indices.breaker.request.limit: 40%` to fail expensive queries fast rather than OOM the node.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `jvm.gc.old.collection_time > 1s/min`, `jvm.mem.heap_used_percent > 75%`, and `es_query_p99 / p50 > 5x` (latency distribution skew indicating GC). Monitor `indices.breaker.request.tripped` counter — any non-zero value means queries are being killed.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a dedicated Search Service for a hotel reservation system Hotel search isn't a simple lookup — it's "hotels within 2km of the Eiffel Tower, sea view, free wifi, sleeps 2, under €300, available June 12–15." That's a geo query plus full-text plus faceted filters plus a date-range availability check, all ranked and returned in under 500ms. Your authoritative SQL database (where bookings and inventory live) *can* answer this, but it would need multi-column indexes on every filter combination and would choke on faceted aggregations like "how many matching hotels have a pool?" — that's a full scan per query. Elasticsearch is purpose-built for exactly this shape of query. ## What happens without it Point search at the SQL primary and two things break. First, the 350 sustained / 1.2K peak search QPS competes with booking writes for the same database — a busy search hour slows down the actual checkout path, and a badly filtered query ("hotels in France") can lock inventory rows or blow the query planner. Second, users see 2–4 second blank result screens on mobile and bounce before they ever reach the hold step. Operators see SQL CPU pegged at 100% while booking latency climbs in sympathy. ## The number Search:Book ratio is **30:1** — 30M searches/day vs 1M booking attempts. At 30M / 86,400 ≈ **350 QPS sustained**, search is ~30x heavier than booking traffic. Isolating that read load onto Elasticsearch (plus a CDN with 60s TTL absorbing most popular queries) keeps the SQL primary free to do the one job only it can do: the guarded inventory decrement that prevents overselling. ## Trade-off The designer accepted eventual consistency on search (ES can lag SQL by tens of seconds) in exchange for fast faceted queries — which is why the API *always* re-checks availability against inventory before creating a hold.

inventory.name: Inventory Service
inventory.summary: Authoritative service managing room-type inventory per hotel per date. Owns the decrement/release logic.

sections.heading: Domain model
sections.body:
```
TABLE room_inventory hotel_id UUID room_type_id UUID date DATE total_rooms INT booked_rooms INT PRIMARY KEY (hotel_id, room_type_id, date)
```
Invariant: `booked_rooms <= total_rooms` enforced by a CHECK constraint.

sections.heading: Decrement on book
sections.body:
Guarded UPDATE inside the booking transaction:
```sql
UPDATE room_inventory
SET booked_rooms = booked_rooms + 1
WHERE hotel_id =? AND room_type_id =? AND date =? AND booked_rooms < total_rooms;
-- 0 rows affected = sold out
```

sections.heading: Hold vs decrement
sections.body: A hold is a Redis lock saying 'this user has the right to try to book this room within 10m'. The inventory decrement happens only on confirmed booking — so an abandoned hold just expires and leaves inventory untouched.

sections.heading: Release on cancel
sections.body: Booking cancellation runs `booked_rooms = booked_rooms - 1` in the same SQL txn as the booking state change.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-row contention on popular hotel-date inventory rows
bottlenecks.trigger: A single trending hotel (conference, concert, holiday weekend) concentrates bookings on the same (hotel_id, room_type_id, date) rows. At 50 peak booking QPS, if even 20% targets one hotel's 3-night stay, ~10 QPS serialize on the same 3 rows via the guarded UPDATE with row-level locks, while each txn also holds the lock through the payment call's p99 = 1.5s.
bottlenecks.symptom: Booking p99 latency on hot hotels balloons past 3–5s; lock wait timeouts surface as `ER_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT` / `deadlock detected` errors in API logs; users on a popular hotel see spinner then 500, while bookings on cold hotels remain fast. `booked_rooms` updates appear to stall.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Do NOT hold the inventory row lock across the payment call. Restructure the flow: (1) payment first with the hold as protection, (2) then a short SQL txn doing only the guarded UPDATE + INSERT bookings + outbox. Keep txns under 25ms. For extremely hot inventory, shard rows into N sub-buckets (`date` + `bucket_id`) so N concurrent bookings can proceed in parallel, then sum buckets for total availability.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `innodb_row_lock_time_avg > 100ms` or `lock_wait_timeout_count > 5/min`. Track `booking_txn_duration_p99` — should stay <50ms; a rise signals the txn is spanning the payment hop. Also monitor `deadlocks_per_min` from `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS`.

bottlenecks.title: Multi-night bookings amplify oversell-guard failures and rollback cost
bottlenecks.trigger: The guarded UPDATE covers all N nights of a stay in one statement (`date IN (...)`). For a 7-night stay, if night 4 is sold out but 1–3 and 5–7 are available, the UPDATE returns `rows_affected=6`, not 7 — requiring detection + ROLLBACK + refund. At 900K bookings/day with avg 3 nights and ~2% contention on any single night during peak season, ~18K/day bookings hit partial-availability rollbacks.
bottlenecks.symptom: Elevated refund rate visible in payment reconciliation; users see a successful hold, card charged, then 'sold out' error after payment — especially for long stays. Operators see `bookings.status='failed'` rows with non-null `charge_id` requiring refund workflow. Inventory utilization appears low because partial decrements are being rolled back.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce strict `rows_affected == N` check before COMMIT; on mismatch, ROLLBACK and trigger async refund using the charge_id as the dedupe key. Ensure the hold TTL (10min) comfortably covers the payment p99 (1.5s) so holds prevent this case in practice — the SQL guard is defense-in-depth only. Add a pre-check `SELECT... FOR UPDATE` on all N rows before payment when hold staleness is suspected (CDC lag >30s).
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `inventory_partial_decrement_rollbacks_per_min`; alert if >5/min. Compare `bookings.status='failed' AND charge_id IS NOT NULL` count per hour against the refund job's success count — divergence means orphaned charges. Track `avg_nights_per_failed_booking` vs successful bookings — a skew toward longer stays confirms this failure mode.

bottlenecks.title: Inventory write bursts saturate CDC pipeline, stalling Search index freshness
bottlenecks.trigger: Every booking and cancellation writes to `room_inventory`, producing ~1.8M inventory row changes/day (900K bookings × 2 nights avg × 1 update, plus cancellations). During flash sales or marketing pushes when booking QPS 5x's from 12 to 60+, the CDC stream from MySQL binlog to Elasticsearch backs up, pushing `last_cdc_lag_s` from 45s baseline toward minutes.
bottlenecks.symptom: Search returns rooms that are already sold out, producing a spike in POST /holds 409 responses; search-to-hold conversion drops. On-call sees CDC consumer lag metric climbing, and Elasticsearch `availability_flag=true` diverges from SQL ground truth by >1% in canary comparisons.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Batch binlog events per (hotel_id, room_type_id) window (5s) so a single hotel's rapid-fire updates become one ES document update, not N. Scale CDC consumer parallelism by `hotel_id % N` partition key. Emit inventory change events to Kafka with short retention but aggressive consumer scaling. Enforce a CDC-lag SLO: alert at 30s, page at 120s; search can fall back to a per-hotel SQL availability re-check for hotels where `booked_rooms/total_rooms > 0.85`.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor `cdc_consumer_lag_seconds` and `binlog_backlog_bytes`. Run a 1% sampled job comparing ES `availability_flag` vs SQL ground truth every 60s; alert on divergence >1%. Track `holds_409_sold_out_ratio` — a sustained rise signals stale search index.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Inventory Service exists for a hotel booking system The whole problem statement hinges on one word: **without overselling**. That means somewhere in this system, there has to be a single source of truth that answers "is room type R at hotel H on date D still available, and if so, claim it atomically." Search can't do this (it's a stale Elasticsearch index, lagging by ~45 seconds). Redis holds can't do this either — they're a soft reservation, and a Redis failover could drop them. The Inventory Service owns the one SQL table (`room_inventory`) with a `CHECK (booked_rooms <= total_rooms)` constraint and the guarded `UPDATE... WHERE booked_rooms < total_rooms` that makes overselling *mathematically impossible*, even under concurrent bookings. ## What happens without it Imagine two guests race to book the last room. Without a centralized, transactional decrement, both see "1 available" in search, both pass the Redis hold check (if holds were keyed slightly differently, or if Redis lost state), both get charged by the payment provider. Now you have two confirmed bookings for one room. The guest who arrives second is walked to a competitor hotel at your expense, you eat a refund plus compensation, and the operator sees angry support tickets and a reputational hit. ## The number Capacity says **900K successful bookings/day → ~50 peak booking QPS**. That's tiny throughput — a single SQL primary handles it easily. The Inventory Service isn't here for scale; it's here because at 900K × 365 × 5 ≈ **1.6B booking rows over 5 years**, even a 0.01% oversell rate = 160K walked guests. Correctness matters more than performance. ## Trade-off The designer accepted a single-primary SQL bottleneck (vs. a distributed store) because strong consistency on one hot row is worth more than horizontal write scale at this QPS.

db.name: Reservation DB (SQL)
db.summary: Strongly-consistent SQL database holding bookings, inventory, and audit trail.

sections.heading: Why SQL
sections.body: Booking is the textbook case for ACID: a booking must be atomic with its inventory decrement and its payment row — or none of them. Eventual consistency = overselling. MySQL/Postgres with row-level locks handle the ~50 peak booking QPS with room to spare.

sections.heading: Schema (simplified)
Transaction
Partitioning
sections.body: bookings partitioned by `YEAR(check_in)` for pruned queries. room_inventory partitioned by `hotel_id % 256` — any single hotel fits comfortably on a single partition.

sections.heading: Replication
sections.body: Synchronous replica in the same region, async across regions. Writes always go to the primary; the replica serves read-your-writes reads with a `read_after_lsn` hint.

gained: Multi-region strong consistency out of the box
lost: More operational complexity than single-primary MySQL

bottlenecks.title: Single primary write ceiling when booking bursts coincide with inventory updates
bottlenecks.trigger: Booking commits serialize through one SQL primary. Each booking writes 1 bookings row + N room_inventory updates (avg 3 nights) + 1 outbox row ≈ 5 writes/booking. At 50 peak booking QPS + cancellations + partner inventory sync + CDC binlog pressure, sustained write volume is ~300-500 writes/sec with fsync per commit; a flash sale or marketing push 5x-ing booking QPS to 250 pushes the primary near its ~2K writes/sec practical limit on a typical r6g.2xlarge Aurora/MySQL instance.
bottlenecks.symptom: Commit latency climbs from <10ms to 100ms+; booking transactions that span the payment hop (1.5s p99) now take 2-3s wall-clock; LB sees /bookings p99 breach 2s SLO; InnoDB `history list length` grows as long-running txns block purge; replica lag on the async cross-region replica balloons past 10s, breaking read-your-writes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Keep booking txns razor-thin: do NOT span the payment call with an open txn (payment first, then short <25ms SQL commit). Move outbox writes to a separate partitioned table with its own tablespace to reduce contention. Provision primary with `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1` but use group commit tuning (`binlog_group_commit_sync_delay=1000`) to batch fsyncs. Pre-scale primary to r6g.4xlarge ahead of known peaks; if sustained growth exceeds single-primary capacity, shard bookings by `hotel_id % N` since cross-hotel writes never need atomicity.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `innodb_log_waits > 0`, `commit_latency_p99 > 50ms` for 2min, `history_list_length > 100K`, and replica `seconds_behind_master > 5s`. Track `writes_per_sec` against a documented ceiling (e.g., 70% of benchmarked max).

bottlenecks.title: Partition pruning failure on bookings queries causes full-table scans
bottlenecks.trigger: `bookings` is partitioned by `YEAR(check_in)` but many common queries filter by `created_at`, `user_id`, or `idempotency_key` — none of which align with the partition key. At 1.6B rows over 5 years, a `SELECT * FROM bookings WHERE user_id =?` without the partition key scans all 5 yearly partitions. The idempotency-key UNIQUE lookup (executed on every POST /bookings retry = 5K/day plus first-attempt checks ~1M/day) does a global unique index lookup, which still works but the index itself grows to ~40GB and competes for buffer pool with hot inventory pages.
bottlenecks.symptom: User booking history page (`WHERE user_id =? ORDER BY created_at DESC`) takes 2-5s; idempotency-key lookups slow from 2ms to 20ms+ as the unique index spills out of buffer pool; InnoDB buffer pool hit ratio drops below 95%; `innodb_buffer_pool_reads` (disk reads) climbs; on-call sees slow-query log filling with bookings-table scans.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a covering secondary index `(user_id, created_at DESC)` with INCLUDE columns for the booking list view. Keep `idempotency_key` as a separate UNIQUE index but consider a secondary Redis cache for hot idempotency lookups (already have Redis for 24h idem cache — ensure SQL is only hit on cache miss). Increase `innodb_buffer_pool_size` to 75% of RAM. For historical bookings (>1yr old), archive to a separate cold partition/table to keep the working set small.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor `innodb_buffer_pool_hit_ratio < 98%`, `slow_query_log` for queries touching bookings without `check_in` in WHERE, and `handler_read_rnd_next` rate (full-scan indicator). Alert if idempotency-key lookup p99 > 10ms.

bottlenecks.title: Outbox table becomes a hot spot and bloats from poller contention
bottlenecks.trigger: Every booking commit inserts 1+ outbox rows (confirmation email, hotel partner push) = ~900K inserts/day baseline + cancellations. The notification worker polls with `SELECT... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100`, which at 12 sustained / 50 peak booking QPS means the poller runs every 1-2s. SKIP LOCKED still acquires and releases row locks on scanned rows; if the worker falls behind (SES/Twilio throttling), undelivered rows pile up and the table grows — at 1M rows/day, a 1-hour outage = 40K rows accumulated, and the poller's LIMIT 100 scan touches increasing numbers of already-locked rows.
bottlenecks.symptom: Outbox poller throughput drops as backlog grows (quadratic degradation); notification email delivery p99 climbs from seconds to minutes; `SELECT... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` query time grows from 5ms to 200ms+; MVCC undo log grows because uncommitted/long-running poller txns block purge; booking commit latency increases as outbox INSERT competes for the same page locks.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Partition outbox by `created_at` day; have the poller drop old delivered partitions rather than DELETE row-by-row. Add index on `(delivered_at, created_at)` with `delivered_at IS NULL` being the hot path — consider a partial index in Postgres. Archive delivered rows to a history table every hour (`DELETE FROM outbox WHERE delivered_at < now - interval '1h' RETURNING * INTO outbox_history`). For higher scale, replace polling with Debezium CDC → Kafka so notification workers consume from Kafka, not SQL. Run multiple poller instances sharded by `id % N`.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `outbox_undelivered_count > 10K`, `outbox_oldest_undelivered_age_seconds > 300`, and poller query time p95 > 50ms. Track `outbox_table_size_bytes` growth rate; should be near zero (steady-state delete catches up with insert).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a SQL database sits at the core of a hotel reservation system The problem statement has one non-negotiable constraint: **never oversell**. That means somewhere in this system, two guests racing for the last room must have exactly one win and one lose — atomically, with no ambiguity. SQL databases give you ACID transactions and row-level locks, which is precisely the tool for this. The booking transaction bundles three things that must succeed or fail together: the guarded inventory decrement (`UPDATE... WHERE booked_rooms < total_rooms`), the INSERT into `bookings` with a UNIQUE idempotency_key, and an outbox row for the confirmation email. Either all three commit, or none do. Redis holds are a softer pre-check, and the search index is stale by tens of seconds — neither can be the source of truth. ## What happens without it Swap SQL for an eventually-consistent store (Cassandra, DynamoDB without conditional writes, etc.) and the failure looks like this: two guests on different API replicas both pass their Redis hold checks (perhaps after a brief Redis failover split-brain), both get charged by Stripe, and both see a confirmation screen. One of them shows up at the hotel and gets "walked" to a competitor at your expense. The operator sees the double-booking in a reconciliation report hours later; support eats the refund, the compensation voucher, and a one-star review. ## The number 900K successful bookings/day × 365 × 5 years ≈ **1.6B booking rows**. At **50 peak booking QPS**, a single SQL primary handles the write load trivially — the `UPDATE` touches one indexed row and commits in ~10ms. The bottleneck here isn't throughput; it's correctness on one hot row. ## Trade-off The designer accepted a single-primary write ceiling (no horizontal write scaling) because at 50 QPS, strong consistency on the oversell guard is worth far more than distributed write throughput.

redis.name: Redis (Holds + Idempotency)
redis.summary: In-memory store for short-lived room holds and idempotency-key result cache.

sections.heading: Hold key
sections.body: `hold:{hotel_id}:{room_type_id}:{date}` → hold_token (UUID). Created via `SET key value NX EX 600` — SETNX + TTL atomically. Only one holder at a time; others get 409 Conflict.

sections.heading: Idempotency-key cache
sections.body: `idem:{key}` → { status, booking_id, response_body }. Populated on the first successful response; TTL 24h. Retries of the same POST /bookings hash-lookup this and return the original response without re-invoking the DB or payment.

sections.heading: Why Redis (not SQL)
sections.body: Holds have TTL (~10 min) and don't need durability — a Redis failover drops them, and the worst case is a user sees 'room no longer held, please retry'. SQL would need a sweeper job to clean expired rows; Redis does it natively via TTL.

sections.heading: Failure semantics
sections.body: Redis cluster with Sentinel / replication. On primary loss, a brief window of double-holds is possible (at most N seconds of unacked writes); the SQL guarded UPDATE is the ultimate oversell protection.

lost: Needs a sweeper job for expiries
Extra pressure on the SQL primary

bottlenecks.title: Redis primary failover drops in-flight holds and idempotency state
bottlenecks.trigger: Redis replication is asynchronous; on primary failure, up to N seconds of unacked writes (typically 1-2s of SETs) are lost during Sentinel failover (~10-30s total unavailability). With 30K concurrent holds and ~5K idempotency retries/day, a failover during peak booking (50 QPS) loses ~50-100 in-flight holds and any in_flight idempotency markers written in the last second.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users mid-checkout see 'hold expired' on submit even though their countdown shows time remaining; concurrent retries that lost their in_flight marker double-submit to the payment provider (saved only by Stripe's own Idempotency-Key dedupe); on-call sees a spike of 409 hold_expired and duplicate charge_id attempts at the payment provider in the minutes following failover.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use Redis with WAIT command (`WAIT 1 100`) on critical idempotency writes to force replication ack before returning, accepting ~2ms latency. Deploy Redis Enterprise or ElastiCache with multi-AZ + automatic failover <15s. Critically, rely on SQL's UNIQUE constraint on `bookings.idempotency_key` as the ultimate dedupe — Redis is an optimization, not the source of truth. For holds, the SQL guarded UPDATE remains the oversell guard even if Redis loses state.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Redis replication lag > 500ms, Sentinel failover events, and any spike in `bookings` INSERT conflicts on `idempotency_key` UNIQUE (indicates cache miss after failover). Track `hold_expired_409_rate` with a 5min window; sudden 10x rise correlates with Redis instability.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-key contention on popular hotel-date hold keys
bottlenecks.trigger: A viral hotel or event concentrates hold attempts on the same `hold:{hotel_id}:{room_type_id}:{date}` keys. At 50 peak booking QPS with 20% targeting one hot hotel's 3-night stay, ~10 QPS hammer the same 3 Redis keys via the all-or-nothing SETNX Lua script. Redis is single-threaded per key; the Lua EVAL blocks the entire shard during execution (~0.5ms each), and at 10+ QPS with 3-key scripts plus GETs from concurrent hold-check operations, the hot shard's CPU climbs fast.
bottlenecks.symptom: P99 latency on hold creation for hot hotels climbs from 3ms to 20-50ms; `redis-cli --latency` shows spikes on the shard hosting the hot keys; `SLOWLOG` fills with EVAL entries; meanwhile other shards are idle. Users on the hot hotel page see slower 'Reserve' button response while cold inventory is snappy.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard by `hotel_id` using Redis Cluster hash tags (`hold:{h-812}:rt-4:date`) so one hotel's keys land on one shard but the cluster spreads hot hotels across nodes. Keep the Lua script small and avoid extra work inside EVAL. For extreme hot spots, use client-side request coalescing: if a SETNX returns fail, wait 50ms before the caller retries rather than thundering. Monitor and be prepared to manually resplit if one hotel dominates.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard CPU alert at >70%, per-key hit rate via `redis-cli --hotkeys`, and `commandstats` for EVAL count skew. Alert when any single shard's ops/sec is >3x the cluster median.

bottlenecks.title: Idempotency key cache growth and eviction under 24h TTL
bottlenecks.trigger: Idempotency keys are cached for 24h. At 1M booking attempts/day + ~5K retries + cancellation idempotency keys, ~1M+ `idem:*` keys accumulate at steady state. Each entry stores the full response body (~1-2 KB including booking_id, confirmation, error details) → ~1-2 GB just for idempotency cache, on top of 30 MB of holds. Under memory pressure with `maxmemory-policy=allkeys-lru`, idempotency entries may evict before their 24h TTL.
bottlenecks.symptom: A client retries a POST /bookings after 12 hours (e.g., mobile app resumed from background) expecting the cached 201 response, but Redis has evicted the key — API treats it as a fresh request, passes through to payment provider which (thanks to its own idempotency) returns the original charge, but the API may double-commit or return inconsistent state. Also, eviction of `in_flight` markers during traffic bursts removes the concurrent-retry guard within the payment window.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Provision Redis with explicit headroom: 4-8 GB per shard for idem cache at steady state; use `maxmemory-policy=volatile-lru` so only TTL'd keys evict (never hold keys). Consider shortening idempotency TTL to 1h for happy-path entries (matches typical retry window) and keep 24h only for terminal-failure entries. Always rely on SQL's UNIQUE `idempotency_key` index as the durable dedupe — on cache miss, API must do a `SELECT... WHERE idempotency_key=?` before proceeding.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `used_memory / maxmemory > 75%`, `evicted_keys > 0/min`, and `keyspace_misses` rate on the `idem:` keyspace. Track a canary metric: ratio of POST /bookings that hit SQL's UNIQUE constraint violation (indicates cache-miss-after-commit path) — should be near zero.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Redis sits between the user and the booking database The hotel system has a tricky UX problem: the user needs 2-4 minutes to type card details, but during those minutes the room must be *reserved for them* — otherwise someone else buys it out from under them and you get the "stole my room" experience. You can't write that reservation to SQL, because an abandoned checkout would leave a junk row that needs a cleanup job. You need something that says "this room is mine to *try* to book for the next 10 minutes" and then forgets on its own. Redis with `SET NX EX 600` does exactly that: atomic claim + automatic expiry. It also caches the `Idempotency-Key` result so a mobile client retrying a flaky POST doesn't trigger a second card charge. ## What happens without it Skip Redis and you have two options, both bad. If you skip holds entirely, two users racing for the last room both make it all the way to the payment screen; one of them pays, the other gets a 409 after entering their card — a furious support ticket. If you put holds in SQL instead, every search-to-checkout click writes and later deletes a row, and you need a sweeper cron; meanwhile the SQL primary (your oversell guard) is busier with disposable work. ## The number Capacity says **30K concurrent holds** at peak (50 booking QPS × 10 min TTL). At ~1 KB per hold, that's **30 MB** — trivial for Redis, but 30K short-lived SQL rows/min churning through your booking primary is painful. ## Trade-off The designer accepted that a Redis failover could drop in-flight holds, because SQL's guarded `UPDATE` is the ultimate oversell guard — Redis is an optimization, not the source of truth.

payment.name: Payment Provider (external)
payment.summary: Third-party payment processor (Stripe / Adyen / Braintree) charging the guest's card.

sections.heading: External SLA
sections.body: Typical provider: p95 ≈ 600 ms, p99 ≈ 1.5 s. Occasionally 3xx ms long for 3D Secure / SCA challenges. Error rate 0.2–1% from transient network + issuer declines.

sections.heading: Idempotency at the network layer
sections.body: Stripe-style: caller sends `Idempotency-Key: uuid` header. A retry of the same POST with the same key returns the original charge (or its final-state result) — never double-charges.

sections.heading: Rate limits
sections.body: Provider-enforced pooled limit (typical: ~200 concurrent in-flight). Budget our booking concurrency to stay below this even at peak.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Decline (insufficient funds) → booking.status = 'failed', hold released immediately
- Network timeout → DO NOT assume failure; check with `GET /charges/{idempotency_key}` before deciding
- Provider-side outage → queue a compensating cancel; explicit user message

gained: Stronger international coverage and local methods
lost: Integration surface is larger than Stripe's

bottlenecks.title: Provider concurrent in-flight pool exhaustion during latency spikes
bottlenecks.trigger: Provider enforces ~200 concurrent in-flight charge limit. Normal load: 50 peak booking QPS × 0.6s p95 = 30 concurrent — comfortable. But when provider p99 degrades to 1.5s or worse (3DS/SCA, provider incident), concurrent in-flight climbs to 75–150+. A brief 3s latency episode under 50 QPS pushes to 150 concurrent, and retry storms from timed-out API calls can breach the 200 ceiling.
bottlenecks.symptom: Provider returns 429 `rate_limit_exceeded` or connection refused on new charge attempts; booking POSTs fail at the payment step with `payment_unavailable`; already-held rooms sit locked for the 10-minute TTL while the user can't pay; conversion drops sharply during the incident window; on-call sees provider concurrent-in-flight metric pegged at 200.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce a client-side semaphore capped at ~150 concurrent calls across all API replicas (leave headroom below the 200 ceiling) using a distributed token bucket in Redis. Bulkhead per-replica to ~40 concurrent. Set aggressive 3s timeouts followed by `GET /charges/{idempotency_key}` reconciliation rather than blind retries. On semaphore wait > 500ms, fail fast with `retry_after` header so clients back off rather than pile on.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `payment_concurrent_inflight > 150` for 1min, `payment_provider_429_rate > 0.1%`, and `payment_call_duration_p99 > 2s` for 2min. Track semaphore wait time p95 — rising above 100ms indicates approaching saturation.

bottlenecks.title: Network timeout ambiguity produces orphaned charges or double-charges
bottlenecks.trigger: At p99 1.5s and occasional 3s+ tails, an API-side timeout (e.g., 3s client cutoff) fires while the provider is still processing. With 1M booking attempts/day and ~0.5% timeout rate, that's ~5000 ambiguous responses/day where the API doesn't know if the charge succeeded. Blind retry → double-charge (mitigated by Idempotency-Key header, but only if key is passed through unchanged). Assume-failure → orphaned charge (card debited, no booking row).
bottlenecks.symptom: Guests report charges without confirmation emails; reconciliation job flags `charge_ids` at provider with no matching `bookings.charge_id`; or in the worse case, `ch_id_A` and `ch_id_B` both exist for the same logical attempt (provider idempotency broke due to key mismatch). Support load spikes during any provider latency event.
bottlenecks.mitigation: NEVER treat a timeout as a definitive failure. On timeout, call `GET /v1/charges?idempotency_key={key}` to resolve true state before deciding. Always pass the client's `Idempotency-Key` unchanged to the provider so dual-layer dedupe protects against retries. Persist a `bookings` row in `pending` state with the idempotency key BEFORE calling payment; a sweeper reconciles pending rows every 60s by polling the provider.
bottlenecks.detection: Reconciliation metric: count of provider charges (last 1h) with no matching `bookings.charge_id` — should be zero within 5min window. Alert on `payment_timeout_rate > 1%` and `bookings_pending_older_than_5min > 0`. Track `distinct_charge_ids_per_idempotency_key` — must be 1.

bottlenecks.title: Elevated decline/error rate (0.2–1%) cascades into user-visible failures and wasted holds
bottlenecks.trigger: Baseline provider error rate is 0.2–1% (issuer declines, transient network errors). At 1M booking attempts/day, that's 2K–10K failures/day. During issuer outages (major card network incident) the rate can spike to 5–10%, meaning at peak 50 QPS, 2.5–5 bookings/second fail at the payment step, each leaving a 10-minute hold locked unless explicitly released.
bottlenecks.symptom: Spike in 402 `card_declined` and `payment_unavailable` responses; bookable inventory appears artificially low because failed attempts leave holds pinned (if release path has bugs); conversion drops; users re-try with different cards creating multiple holds on the same inventory. Error budget on `/bookings` success rate blown for the day.
bottlenecks.mitigation: On any terminal payment failure, immediately release the Redis hold keys (pipelined DEL) so inventory frees up before the TTL. Cache the 402 response under the idempotency key with 24h TTL so blind retries don't re-hit the provider. Implement a fallback to a secondary provider (e.g., Adyen as backup to Stripe) triggered by circuit breaker when primary error rate > 5% over 2min. Surface specific decline reasons to the UI so users can correct (wrong CVV) vs try another card (insufficient funds).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `payment_decline_rate > 2%` over 5min (baseline is ~1%), `payment_5xx_rate > 0.5%`, and `holds_released_due_to_payment_failure_rate` spikes. Segment by `decline_code` to detect issuer-specific incidents early.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why an external payment provider for a hotel reservation system Hotels need to actually collect money before a booking counts as confirmed — that's the whole point of the "confirm" step in hold-then-confirm. But taking card numbers directly means becoming PCI-DSS compliant, handling 3D Secure challenges, integrating with every card network and issuer bank, and dealing with chargebacks. That's a multi-year engineering investment just to do a side quest to the real problem (inventory + no-oversell). Stripe/Adyen/Braintree have already built all of this, and critically, they give you a **network-grade `Idempotency-Key` header** — the exact primitive needed so that a mobile client retrying a flaky POST doesn't double-charge the guest. ## What happens without it Build payments in-house and two things go wrong fast. First, you're storing card PANs, which means any breach is catastrophic and you need yearly PCI audits. Second, without a battle-tested idempotency layer, a network timeout during the charge call leaves you guessing: did the card get charged or not? Retry blindly → double-charge, support tickets, chargebacks. Assume failure → orphaned money, the guest is debited with no booking row, and reconciliation is a manual mess. ## The number 1M booking attempts/day with a ~0.5% transient error rate = **5,000 retries/day** where idempotency is load-bearing. Provider p99 is **1.5s**; at 50 peak booking QPS × 1.5s = **75 concurrent in-flight charges**, well under the ~200 pooled limit — but a provider slowdown to 3s pushes this to 150, why bulkheading matters. ## Trade-off You accept external dependency and per-transaction fees (~2.9% + 30¢) in exchange for not owning PCI scope or card-network integrations.

notify.name: Notification Service
notify.summary: Async worker that reads the outbox table and sends email / SMS / push confirmations.

sections.heading: Transactional outbox
sections.body: Booking commit writes a row to `outbox` in the same transaction as the booking. A separate poller picks up new rows, dispatches, and marks them delivered. This guarantees at-least-once notification — and never blocks the booking response.

sections.heading: Channels
sections.body: Email via SES/SendGrid, SMS via Twilio, push via APNs/FCM. Each has its own retry policy; final failures go to a human-reviewed queue.

sections.heading: Why not synchronous
sections.body: External email/SMS providers are noisy — retries would balloon booking latency. User-visible latency is paid only for payment, which is unavoidable.

bottlenecks.title: Outbox poller lag during notification provider throttling or outages
bottlenecks.trigger: SES/Twilio rate limits or provider incidents slow delivery below ingestion rate. At 900K bookings/day + cancellations ≈ 1M+ outbox rows/day (~12 sustained, ~50 peak/sec), a 1-hour SES throttling incident accumulates ~40K undelivered rows. Poller uses `SELECT... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100` which scans over locked/failed rows, degrading quadratically as backlog grows.
bottlenecks.symptom: Confirmation emails arrive minutes-to-hours after booking instead of seconds; users call support thinking the booking failed; on-call sees `outbox.delivered_at IS NULL` row count climbing; poller query time grows from 5ms to 200ms+; MVCC undo log bloats from long-running poller transactions, secondarily slowing booking commits on the same SQL primary.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Partition outbox by `created_at` day and add a partial index `WHERE delivered_at IS NULL` (Postgres) or equivalent covering index. Run N poller workers sharded by `id % N` to parallelize. Per-channel circuit breakers: on SES 429, back off that channel only while still draining SMS/push. Separate retry queue for repeatedly-failed rows so they don't block the head-of-line. Archive delivered rows hourly to keep the hot set small.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `outbox_undelivered_count > 10K`, `outbox_oldest_undelivered_age_seconds > 300`, poller query p95 > 50ms, and per-channel provider error rate > 2% over 5min.

bottlenecks.title: Duplicate notifications from at-least-once delivery without dedupe
bottlenecks.trigger: Outbox guarantees at-least-once: worker sends via SES/Twilio, then UPDATEs `delivered_at`. If the worker crashes between send and UPDATE (~100-300ms window per send at 50-300ms service time), the row stays `NULL` and another worker redelivers. At 1M+ outbox rows/day and worker restart frequency during deploys (multiple/day), expect dozens to hundreds of duplicate sends/day.
bottlenecks.symptom: Guests receive 2-3 identical confirmation emails or SMS for one booking; support tickets 'why was I charged multiple times?' (even though only 1 charge exists); SMS costs inflate (Twilio charges per send); spam complaints hurt SES sender reputation score, risking deliverability throttling.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a provider-level idempotency/dedupe key: SES `X-SES-MESSAGE-TAGS` + `Message-ID` derived from `outbox.id`; Twilio supports idempotency via `Idempotency-Key` header. Commit `delivered_at` BEFORE the external call is impossible, so instead persist `attempt_id` and use provider dedupe. For channels without dedupe, add a `sent_message_id` column updated atomically after send; skip if already set on worker restart.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `duplicate_send_ratio` by comparing distinct `outbox.id` to send count in provider logs; alert if >0.1%. Monitor SES complaint rate (target <0.1%) and bounce rate (<5%) as a leading indicator of deliverability damage.

bottlenecks.title: Poller contention adds write pressure and lock waits on the SQL primary
bottlenecks.trigger: Every successful booking commit writes 1+ outbox rows (~900K/day baseline) on the same SQL primary handling the 50 peak booking QPS with <25ms txn budget. Poller runs `SELECT... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` every 1-2s and then `UPDATE outbox SET delivered_at = now`. At peak, poller + booking commits compete for the same table pages and buffer pool entries; index writes on `(delivered_at)` re-balance during heavy delete/update churn.
bottlenecks.symptom: Booking commit latency p99 creeps up 10-30ms during notification bursts; `innodb_row_lock_time_avg` rises on outbox pages; buffer pool hit ratio drops as outbox history pages compete with hot `room_inventory` and `bookings` pages; unrelated booking transactions see elevated lock waits.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Move outbox to a separate tablespace or even a dedicated smaller SQL instance fed by logical replication, so polling churn can't touch booking primary pages. Longer-term, replace polling with Debezium CDC → Kafka: binlog-tail the outbox commits and have notification workers consume from Kafka, zero query load on the primary. Delete delivered rows in bulk hourly rather than row-by-row.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor `innodb_buffer_pool_hit_ratio` on outbox pages, `booking_commit_p99` correlated with `outbox_poller_qps`, and `outbox_table_size_bytes` (should be near-flat at steady state). Alert if booking commit p99 rises while booking QPS is flat.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Notification Service for a hotel reservation system In this design, the booking request has already done a lot of slow work by the time we reach "send the confirmation email": a Redis hold check, a payment provider round-trip (p99 = 1.5s), and a SQL transaction. If we *also* made the user wait for SES or Twilio to accept the email before returning `201 Confirmed`, we'd be chaining yet another flaky external call onto an already-tight latency budget. Worse, if SES is throttling, the booking — which is already safely committed in SQL and paid for — would appear to fail from the user's perspective. The Notification Service decouples "the booking is real" from "the email got sent," using the transactional outbox pattern so both happen reliably but independently. ## What happens without it If the API sent email synchronously and SES had a hiccup, the user would see a spinner, then a timeout, then an error page — even though their card was charged and the booking row exists in SQL. They'd retry, hit the idempotency cache, get the same error, and flood support with "did my booking go through?" tickets. Meanwhile the operator sees booking success rate drop purely because of an unrelated email provider issue. ## The number At **900K successful bookings/day ≈ 10 confirmation emails/sec sustained**, plus cancellations and reminders, that's ~1M+ outbound messages/day. Email providers routinely have 300ms+ tail latencies and transient 5xx errors at ~0.2% — synchronously, that'd add ~2,000 user-visible failures/day on a path that already succeeded. ## Trade-off The designer accepted "email may arrive seconds-to-minutes late" in exchange for never letting notification failures break the booking path.

operations.title: Search available rooms
operations.name: Search available rooms
operations.description: User searches for hotels; the API queries the search index and returns price + availability cards.

steps.title: User submits a search
steps.action: User fills destination + dates + guests and submits.
steps.codeOrCommand:
GET /search?dest=Paris&checkin=2026-06-12&checkout=2026-06-15&guests=2 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.hotels.example

steps.title: LB routes to an API replica
steps.action: Round-robin / least-connections across healthy API replicas. TLS terminated at LB.

steps.title: API validates and forwards to search
steps.action: Validates date range (check_out > check_in, within 2 years), normalizes destination to a geo bbox (from a cached gazetteer), and delegates to the search service.
steps.codeOrCommand:
if checkout <= checkin: return 400
bbox = gazetteer.lookup("Paris") # cached
results = search.query( geo=bbox, checkin=checkin, checkout=checkout, guests=guests, filters=req.query.filters, page=0, size=20
)

steps.title: Elasticsearch resolves availability + geo + facets
steps.action: ES runs a bool query combining geo_bounding_box, range on check-in/-out, and availability flag. Returns top-20 hotels with price and amenity facets.

steps.title: API shapes the response
steps.action: Adds room-type cards, strikes-through prices, loyalty flags. Returns to client.
steps.codeOrCommand:
return 200, [ { hotel_id, name, img, price_total, price_per_night, rating, amenities, rooms: [{room_type_id, name, price, refundable}] },...
]

steps.title: Client renders result cards
steps.action: Browser shows hotel cards. User clicks one to see detail and eventually initiates a hold.

operations.title: Book (hold → pay → confirm, with idempotency)
operations.name: Book (hold → pay → confirm, with idempotency)
operations.description: Happy-path booking: client creates a hold, then POST /bookings with an Idempotency-Key, API charges payment, commits DB, releases hold, and enqueues notification.

steps.title: Client creates a hold before checkout
steps.action: When user clicks 'Reserve' on a room, client POSTs /holds to reserve it for 10 minutes while they enter payment details.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /holds HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json {"hotel_id":"h-812","room_type_id":"rt-4","checkin":"2026-06-12","checkout":"2026-06-15"}

steps.title: API asks Redis for a hold
steps.action: API generates a hold_token (UUID) and attempts to SETNX one key per night so partial holds aren't possible — all-or-nothing.
steps.codeOrCommand:
hold_token = uuid4
keys = [f"hold:h-812:rt-4:{d}" for d in nights]
# Lua script: all-or-nothing SETNX + EX across N keys
SCRIPT = """
for i,k in ipairs(KEYS) do if redis.call('EXISTS', k) == 1 then for j=1,i-1 do redis.call('DEL', KEYS[j]) end return 0 end redis.call('SET', k, ARGV[1], 'NX', 'EX', 600)
end
return 1
"""
ok = redis.eval(SCRIPT, keys=keys, argv=[hold_token])

steps.title: Redis commits hold keys
steps.action: Each night's key is atomically claimed with a 10-minute TTL. Returns 1 (success).

steps.title: API returns hold_token and expiry
steps.action: Client will pass hold_token with the eventual POST /bookings. Countdown starts on the UI.

steps.title: User enters payment info, submits booking with Idempotency-Key
steps.action: User types card info. Client generates a fresh UUID as `Idempotency-Key` and sends POST /bookings. Same key is reused on every retry of this booking.

steps.title: API checks idempotency-key cache
steps.action: Before doing any work, API looks up the idempotency key in Redis. Hit → return cached response unchanged (never double-charge). Miss → proceed and mark 'in-flight'.
steps.codeOrCommand:
cached = redis.get(f"idem:{idem_key}")
if cached and cached['status'] in ('confirmed','failed'): return cached['response'] # exact replay
if cached and cached['status'] == 'in_flight': return 409, { error: 'duplicate in flight' }
redis.set(f"idem:{idem_key}", { status: 'in_flight' }, NX, EX=30)
steps.decision: idempotency key already seen — return cached result
steps.note: This branch is taken on retries from a flaky client; the cached result means we do NOT re-run payment. On first submission we fall through.

steps.title: API validates hold_token and begins work
steps.action: Verifies Redis hold keys still hold our token (defense-in-depth; TTL could have expired). If token mismatch → 409 and error.
steps.codeOrCommand: for d in nights: if redis.get(f"hold:h-812:rt-4:{d}")!= hold_token: redis.set(f"idem:{idem_key}", {status:'failed', reason:'hold_expired'}, EX=86400) return 409, { error: 'hold_expired' }

steps.title: API calls payment provider (slow network hop)
steps.action: API calls Stripe-style Charge API with its own idempotency key derived from ours. External service; 200–800 ms typical.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST https://api.paymentprov.com/v1/charges
Idempotency-Key: 3a7f-1e9c-booking
Authorization: Bearer sk_live_***
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded amount=54000&currency=eur&source=tok_visa_4242&
description=Hotel+h-812+rt-4+2026-06-12

steps.title: API opens SQL txn and decrements inventory
steps.action: Inside a BEGIN/COMMIT, runs the guarded decrement for each night. Zero rows affected on any night = sold out → ROLLBACK and refund path.

steps.title: DB writes booking + outbox rows, commits
steps.action: Within the same transaction, INSERT the booking row (with the idempotency_key as a UNIQUE column) and an outbox row for the confirmation email. COMMIT.

steps.title: Release holds + cache idempotency result (parallel)
steps.action: After commit, API deletes the hold keys (someone else may rebook the room the moment a guest cancels) and caches the final idempotency-key result.

steps.title: Outbox worker sends confirmation email (async)
steps.action: A separate worker polls outbox, picks up the new row, and sends the confirmation via SES. Marks delivered. This is off-path from the user — they already have their response.

steps.title: Client receives 201 with confirmation_code
steps.action: User sees success page. The email arrives seconds later.

operations.title: Cancel booking (release inventory)
operations.name: Cancel booking (release inventory)
operations.description: User cancels before check-in; API refunds via payment provider, releases the inventory rows, and notifies the hotel.

steps.title: User taps Cancel
steps.action: Client POSTs to cancel endpoint. Uses a fresh Idempotency-Key on this request so a retry is safe.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /bookings/bk_9x.../cancel HTTP/1.1
Idempotency-Key: 91de-cancel-7
Authorization: Bearer <user-token>

steps.title: API checks idempotency and fetches booking
steps.action: Cache lookup, then read booking row. Must be in `confirmed` state and within the cancellation window per hotel policy.
steps.codeOrCommand:
cached = redis.get(f"idem:{idem_key}")
if cached and cached['status'] == 'cancelled': return cached['response'] row = db.query("SELECT * FROM bookings WHERE booking_id=%s FOR UPDATE", [id])
if row.status!= 'confirmed': return 409
if now > cancellation_deadline(row): return 403
steps.decision: Idempotency-key hit — return cached 200 without re-running refund

steps.title: API refunds via payment provider
steps.action: Issues a refund on the original charge_id. Idempotency-Key ensures a retried refund does not double-refund.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST https://api.paymentprov.com/v1/refunds
Idempotency-Key: 91de-cancel-7 charge=ch_1ABcDeF

steps.title: API releases inventory in SQL txn
steps.action: Transactional: decrement booked_rooms back, mark booking as cancelled, write outbox row for hotel + guest notifications.
steps.codeOrCommand:
BEGIN;
UPDATE room_inventory
SET booked_rooms = booked_rooms - 1
WHERE hotel_id = 'h-812' AND room_type_id = 'rt-4' AND date IN ('2026-06-12','2026-06-13','2026-06-14'); UPDATE bookings
SET status = 'cancelled', updated_at = now
WHERE booking_id = 'bk_9x...'; INSERT INTO outbox (event_type, payload)
VALUES ('booking_cancelled', JSON_OBJECT('booking_id','bk_9x...','refund_id','re_2XyZ123')); COMMIT;

steps.title: DB persists the cancelled state
steps.action: Commit durable. Replica catches up under 1s. Bookings and inventory are consistent.

steps.title: Notifications dispatched (async)
steps.action: Outbox worker picks up the cancellation event, emails the guest with a confirmation of refund, and pushes a message to the hotel's partner channel.
steps.codeOrCommand:
ses.send(to=guest_email, template='booking_cancelled', {booking_id, refund_id});
partner_channel.push({hotel_id, booking_id, event:'cancelled'});

steps.title: Client shows 'Cancellation confirmed'
steps.action: User sees the cancellation screen with the refund reference. Total wall-clock typically 800–1500 ms, dominated by the payment refund hop.

operations.title: Book — payment declined path
operations.name: Book — payment declined path
operations.description: Alternate booking flow where the payment provider declines the card. API releases the hold and caches the failed idempotency-key result so retries are honest.

steps.title: Client submits booking
steps.action: Same as happy path: POST /bookings with hold_token and Idempotency-Key.

steps.title: API miss on idempotency-key, proceeds
steps.action: First attempt; cache miss; marks in-flight and continues.
steps.codeOrCommand: redis.set(f"idem:{idem_key}", { status: 'in_flight' }, NX, EX=30)

steps.title: Payment provider DECLINES
steps.action: Card declined by issuer (insufficient funds). Provider returns 402 with `code=card_declined`.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST https://api.paymentprov.com/v1/charges... → 402 Payment Required
{ "error": { "type": "card_error", "code": "card_declined", "decline_code": "insufficient_funds", "charge": "ch_declined_88" } }
steps.decision: payment declined — DO NOT decrement inventory, release hold and fail fast

steps.title: API releases hold + caches failed idempotency result
steps.action: Same hold keys are deleted so the room is immediately available to another shopper. The idempotency-key result is written as a terminal 'failed' state with the error body — retries of the same key return the same 402 without re-attempting the card.

steps.title: Client shows 'Card declined, please try another'
steps.action: HTTP 402 surfaced to the UI. The user can correct the card and submit again — which will use a NEW Idempotency-Key (since it's a new logical booking attempt).

tradeoffs.decision: Holds in Redis with TTL vs holds as rows in the inventory DB
tradeoffs.rationale: Hold traffic is dominated by expirations and short-lived keys. TTL on Redis is O(1) and kernel-driven; implementing TTL in the inventory DB requires a sweeper and writes amplify under peak booking load. Correctness still lives in the SQL transaction, so Redis is an advisory lock.

tradeoffs.decision: Isolation level for the inventory transaction
tradeoffs.rationale: Booking volume is low (50 peak QPS), so the throughput cost of SERIALIZABLE is negligible; the correctness benefit is that overlapping transactions cannot both see available > 0 and both commit. Payment is kept outside the transaction to avoid holding locks across a 1.5 s external call.

tradeoffs.decision: Second line of defense for oversell: row-lock vs optimistic version
tradeoffs.chosen: Optimistic locking via version column with retry loop
tradeoffs.rationale: For high-demand room types where many requests race on the same row, SELECT... FOR UPDATE serializes them and tanks throughput. An optimistic version column with a bounded retry loop converts contention into user-visible 409 Conflict and keeps the database hot path lock-free.

tradeoffs.chosen: Client-generated UUID scoped to a single hold token
tradeoffs.rationale: Tying the key to hold_token rather than request-id means a retry of the same booking attempt returns the same result, but editing a card after a decline rotates the key. This prevents both double-charges and stuck 402 replays from a 24 h cache.

tradeoffs.chosen: Eventually consistent search from a denormalized cache, authoritative check at hold
tradeoffs.rationale: Search is 30x more traffic than booking. Serving it from the source of truth would waste DB capacity on an operation that the user is not committing to yet. Authoritative check moves to hold time where it belongs.
